implementation_notes: The language itself performs the interception: new Proxy(target, handler) creates an object whose internal methods ([[Get]], [[Set]], [[HasProperty]], [[OwnPropertyKeys]], [[Call]], [[Construct]] and others) run the handler's traps, and Reflect supplies the default forwarding behaviour for each trap. A generated proxy class is therefore unnecessary; the classic form only returns for membranes that must be revocable (Proxy.revocable) or when the target's non-configurable, non-writable properties constrain what the traps may report.
pitfalls: Invariants are enforced: a get, has or ownKeys trap that lies about a non-configurable or non-writable target property makes the operation throw a TypeError.
Private fields and prototype getters see the wrong receiver through a proxy, so traps must pass receiver to Reflect instead of reading target[prop] directly.
Calling Reflect on the proxy rather than the target re-enters the trap and recurses until the stack overflows.

variants.name: pre-ES2015 accessor membrane
variants.implementation_notes: Before ES2015 the same interception was approximated by redefining accessors with Object.defineProperty on the object or on a copy of it, which can trap reads and writes of existing properties but cannot intercept property addition, deletion, the in operator, ownKeys or calls. It mutates or shadows the target instead of virtualising it, so it survives only in legacy runtimes and in libraries that must support them.
pitfalls: Property addition and deletion are invisible: a new key on the target never reaches the membrane, and delete leaves the accessor in place.
The accessors are own properties of the wrapper, so identity, descriptors and Object.keys/for..in behaviour diverge from the target.
